chunks: The compiler of this book said:

Al-Aq'as is the diminutive of al-Aq'as, and that is the one whose neck is curved. Al-Qa'as is a curvature that takes hold in the neck from a wind, as if it breaks it towards what is behind it. Al-Aq'as is the noble, the refraining one. It is also said: 'Azz Aq'as' (He is noble and refraining). Al-Qaw'as is the one with a thick neck, rigorous in his back in all things. Al-Qa'ous is the old man. Al-Qa's is the opposite of hunchbackedness. The verb is: Qa'sa yaq'su qas'an (he was swaybacked). The plural is Qasawāt and Qu's. Al-Qa'sa' is the ant that raises its chest and tail. Al-Aq'nās is intensity. Al-Taqā'us is from 'Such-a-person slacked' if he did not accomplish and did not move forward in what he was assigned to. Muqā'is is a tribe from Tamim.

key_terms.التَّقَاعُسُ: Slacking; failing to accomplish assigned tasks
key_terms.الْأَقْعَسُ: The one with a curved neck; diminutive form
key_terms.الْقَعْسَاءُ: A type of ant that raises its chest and tail

ai.seo_question: What is the linguistic meaning and definition of Al-Aq'as and Al-Taqā'us in Shia scholarly texts?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq provides a precise lexical dissection of the root Q-F-S to elucidate the term 'Al-Aq'as' (the belittled lordotic), distinguishing between physical curvature of the neck and the metaphorical sense of being 'exalted' or 'resistant' (Aziz al-Muntan). This etymological clarification is crucial for understanding the specific honorific or descriptive nuance applied to the Imam in the chapter, grounding the theological title in tangible physical attributes of strength and distinctiveness.
